title: World Model Design and Control Check

questions.question: Why does a partially observable task need a belief state rather than only the latest observation?
options: A belief state combines observation history and actions to represent hidden possibilities that the latest observation cannot distinguish.
A belief state guarantees that every hidden variable becomes directly observable.
A belief state removes the need for an observation model.
A belief state is only a compressed copy of the latest image.
questions.explanation: A belief state summarizes evidence across time and actions, including uncertainty about hidden state. It does not make partial observability disappear.

questions.question: What must an action-conditioned dynamics model predict?
options: How the latent state distribution changes under each candidate action.
Only what usually happens when no action is taken.
Only the visual texture of the current observation.
The final policy weights without any transition model.
questions.explanation: Planning is counterfactual: the model must distinguish the consequences of different candidate actions from the same inferred state.

questions.question: Why can a model with strong one-step accuracy still fail during a long rollout?
options: Its own predictions become later inputs, so small errors can move the rollout into unsupported states and change action rankings.
One-step accuracy always implies perfect multi-step accuracy.
Long rollouts use fewer model predictions than short rollouts.
A planner ignores every state after the first prediction.
questions.explanation: Open-loop imagination feeds predicted state back into the model. Distribution shift and local errors can therefore accumulate with horizon.

questions.question: What is the key control property of receding-horizon model-predictive control?
options: Optimize a sequence, execute its first action, observe the real next state, and plan again.
Execute the full imagined sequence without observing the environment.
Use only a visual reconstruction score to choose actions.
Keep the rollout horizon fixed even when uncertainty rises.
questions.explanation: Replanning after limited execution repeatedly anchors the controller to real evidence and limits exposure to a stale imagined trajectory.

questions.question: How does MuZero differ from a world model trained to reconstruct future images?
options: MuZero learns latent transitions and reward, policy, and value predictions useful for search without requiring observation reconstruction.
MuZero uses no learned dynamics model.
MuZero can plan only when given the complete environment rules.
MuZero predicts images but not rewards or values.
questions.explanation: MuZero learns a value-equivalent latent model: its predictions are optimized for planning quantities rather than pixel reconstruction.

questions.question: An ensemble shows rising disagreement and the proposed plan crosses a hard safety-risk limit. What should the controller do?
options: Reject the plan and use a defined fallback or gather new real evidence before replanning.
Ignore the boundary because predicted return is high.
Increase the open-loop horizon so disagreement averages out.
Treat low reconstruction loss as proof that the action is safe.
questions.explanation: Hard constraints take precedence over imagined return. Uncertainty and boundary violations should trigger containment, fallback, or new evidence.

questions.question: Which evaluation most directly tests whether a world model supports planning?
options: Whether model and reality preserve candidate action rankings across held-out regimes and rollout depths.
Whether generated frames are colorful.
Whether training loss decreases on the replay buffer.
Whether the latent state has the largest possible dimension.
questions.explanation: Planning depends on comparative consequences. Action-ranking agreement connects model predictions to the decisions they are intended to support.
